title: Camp 2 close: the whole life
hookLine: from the palace to the sal trees, from the hare to the prince: stories that teach by being remembered

lines: A QUEEN, A DREAM, A WHITE ELEPHANT.
THE LAST DAY OF THE STORIES.
cards: A queen asleep, dreaming of a white elephant: that's where this camp began, on day twenty-two. You didn't know then who Channa was, or Kanthaka, or Sujata.

You'd never heard of Kisa Gotami or the man with the finger garland. Now, if someone at dinner said the Buddha just sat under a tree and got enlightened, you could tell them about the six years first.
The handful of beans. The bowl that floated upstream. That's what stories do.
They don't argue. They move in and stay. Today, the last day of the stories, walk the whole life once more, from the palace to the sal trees.

teach.b: Walk it with me. A child born in a grove at Lumbini, and an old sage who weeps because he won't live to hear him teach. A prince named Siddhattha, the one whose aim succeeds, in three palaces built to keep sorrow out.
Then four sights through the gate: an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a calm wanderer. A son named Rahula. A sleeping palace, one look back, a horse named Kanthaka, and hair cut with a sword.

teach.h: THE GOING FORTH AND THE HARD YEARS.
teach.b: Two teachers, then six hard years with five companions, down to a handful of beans, until he remembered a quiet afternoon under a rose-apple tree.
Sujata's rice. Eight handfuls of grass, a vow, Mara's army, and a hand touching the earth. Dawn, and a new word: Buddha, awake.
Then the Deer Park, the wheel set turning, Kondañña seeing, the sangha growing, and the women who asked to join and were ordained.
The hard stories: a murderer who stopped, a mother with a mustard seed, Patacara who lost everything and found her feet.

teach.h: THE TEACHING, THE LAST DAYS, THE JATAKA.
teach.b: Eighty years, dipa, Cunda's meal, two sal trees, and the last words: strive on.

Then the Jataka, the lives before, told by the tradition as the long road here: sasa, the hare in the moon, the deer who saved his betrayer, the prince who gave until it hurt, the prince who stayed silent, the prince who swam.
Stories don't teach the way lists do. They teach by being remembered at the right moment.
You don't just know about him now. You know him.

how: Buddhists learn the Buddha's life through retelling: in sermons, temple murals, children's books and festival plays, the same stories are told again and again until they're known by heart.

s: the Buddha awakened the first time he sat down to meditate

the camp ended with the Buddha's last words
the life ended there, but the camp went on into the Jataka, closing with Vessantara, Temiya and Mahajanaka.

games.q: a friend says the Buddha just sat under a tree one day and got enlightened. what do you tell them?
o: that's right, it was that simple.
first came six hard years, then a middle way, then the tree.
nobody knows anything about his life.
games.why: the stories tell of years of extreme practice before he turned to the middle way and sat under the bodhi tree.

practice: Let the stories pass through your mind like pictures on a wall: the elephant, the gate, the tree, the bowl, the sal trees. Don't hold any of them; just notice which one stays a little longer than the others.
That's the one to carry, so breathe with it and see its details: where it happened, who was there, what was said.

wordCard.voice: Jataka. A birth story: one of the tales of the Buddha's earlier lives, which close this camp of seventy-five days, the whole life and the lives before it.

carryVoice: Your line: you know him now. Seventy-five days of stories, and they're yours to keep. Tomorrow, the practices begin.
